story.headline: Committee backs EU treaty, keeps double majority
story.summary: The Council of States' committees advanced the Bilaterals III EU package but reaffirmed it must clear a double majority of voters and cantons.
story.display_body: On Friday 4 September the Council of States' preparatory committees advanced the "Bilaterals III" treaty package with the EU — but reaffirmed that it should have to clear a double hurdle to pass. The relevant committee recommended the government's package — 18 treaties meant to stabilise and extend Switzerland's relations with the EU — for adoption by 9 votes to 3 with one abstention. Separately, the chamber's state-policy committee (SPK-S — the Council of States body that handles domestic implementation) reaffirmed, on the casting vote of its president Heidi Z'graggen (Mitte), that the package must require a double majority (Volks- und Ständemehr — approval by both a majority of voters and a majority of the 26 cantons), and would write a transitional clause into the constitution to that end; the National Council's counterpart committee has backed the same demand. A cantonal majority is a markedly higher bar than the simple popular vote the Federal Council originally envisaged, because it over-weights small rural cantons; opponents led by the SVP have pushed for it precisely because it makes the deal easier to defeat at the ballot box. The full Council of States takes up the package in the autumn session, with a first vote expected by the end of September.
story.why: whether the EU package needs one majority or two could decide the fate of a deal that would shape free movement, market access and Swiss–EU relations for a generation. (moneycab, 04.09.2026; cash, 04.09.2026)

story.headline: Swiss Patriot deal with Germany collapses
story.summary: Switzerland's fallback to obtain Patriot air-defence units sooner via Germany fell through, delaying the first unit to 2032 and raising costs.
story.display_body: Switzerland's attempt to get its Patriot air-defence systems sooner via Germany has collapsed, the federal arms office confirmed on Thursday 3 September, delaying the first unit to 2032 and pushing costs sharply higher. The US had earlier diverted Patriot (a US-made surface-to-air missile system) deliveries away from Switzerland to backfill Germany, which had passed its own batteries to Ukraine; Bern had hoped Berlin would hand over part of its allocation to close the gap. Armaments chief Urs Loher said the options with Germany "cannot be implemented as such". The first Swiss fire unit is now expected in 2032 rather than 2026, and reporting puts the additional cost at between 1.7 and 4.3 billion francs.
story.why: it leaves Switzerland without a modern ground-based air defence for the better part of a decade and adds a multi-billion-franc bill to an already contested procurement. (20 Minuten, 04.09.2026; SRF, 04.09.2026)

story.headline: All five acquitted in Bondo rockslide trial
story.summary: A Graubünden regional court acquitted all five defendants over the 2017 Bondo rockslide that killed eight hikers.
story.display_body: A Graubünden regional court acquitted all five defendants on Friday 4 September in the trial over the 2017 Bondo rockslide, which killed eight hikers. The Regionalgericht Maloja, sitting in Pontresina, cleared the former mayor of Bregaglia and FDP national councillor Anna Giacometti, a municipal forester, two cantonal officials (a geologist and a forestry engineer) and an external geologist, all charged in connection with negligent homicide. The court found no proof of a specific breach of duty of care: in the weeks before the 23 August 2017 collapse at Piz Cengalo there were no clear signs of a foreseeable major event, and — invoking "in dubio pro reo" (when in doubt, for the accused) — it held the calculations and warnings in place at the time were defensible. It nonetheless criticised the absence of an emergency plan that would have included closing the trails. Lead prosecutor Bruno Ulmi Stuppani said an appeal was still open and would be discussed internally.
story.why: the verdict draws a hard line on when officials can be held criminally liable for failing to foresee a natural-hazard disaster, and reopens the question of who is responsible for danger assessment between cantons and municipalities. (20 Minuten liveticker, 04.09.2026)

story.headline: Missouri court blocks Trump-backed House map
story.summary: Missouri's Supreme Court unanimously blocked a Trump-backed congressional map and ordered a statewide referendum, keeping the old map for November.
story.display_body: Missouri's Supreme Court unanimously blocked a Trump-backed redraw of the state's US House map on Thursday 3 September and ordered the new lines put to a statewide referendum. The court ruled that Missouri's constitutional right to a referendum on "any act" of the legislature covers congressional redistricting, so the 2025 GOP-drawn map "did not go into effect and will not go into effect unless and until approved by the voters"; the map drawn after the 2020 census "remains in full force and effect for the November 2026 general election". A group called People Not Politicians had gathered more than 300,000 signatures to force the vote. Republican Attorney General Catherine Hanaway said she would appeal to the US Supreme Court.
story.why: it is a rare courtroom setback in the national mid-decade redistricting fight and denies Republicans a seat they had counted on to defend a slim House majority in the November midterms. (CNN, 03.09.2026; Missouri Independent, 03.09.2026)

story.headline: Meloni sets Italy's postwar longevity record
story.summary: Giorgia Meloni's coalition became the longest continuously serving government of Italy's postwar republic at 1,413 days.
story.display_body: Giorgia Meloni's coalition became the longest continuously serving government in Italy's postwar republic on Friday 4 September, at 1,413 days in office. Italy has cycled through 68 governments in 80 years — about 13 months each on average — so the milestone is real; analysts caution that longevity is not the same as stability. Meloni's Brothers of Italy party, which has post-Fascist roots, planned a rally in Bari in the evening, effectively an early launch for the 2027 election. The government points to figures it claims — around a million more people in work, unemployment below 6%, and a €21 billion cut in personal income taxes — though these are the coalition's own framing of its record.
story.why: durability gives Rome unusual weight in EU negotiations and signals that Europe's hard-right governments can be the norm rather than a passing phase. (DW, 04.09.2026; Al Jazeera, 04.09.2026)

story.headline: Milei escalates Argentina's Falklands claim
story.summary: Argentina's Milei said 'winds of change' back its Falklands claim and threatened faster oil sanctions; UK ministers rejected it.
story.display_body: Argentine President Javier Milei escalated Buenos Aires' claim to the Falkland Islands on Thursday–Friday, saying "winds of change" now favour Argentina and threatening faster sanctions on British oil interests. Milei cited a suggestion by Donald Trump that Washington might reconsider its backing for British sovereignty over the islands, which the UK has governed since long before the 1982 war. British ministers rejected the claim outright, restating that the Falklands' sovereignty is not up for negotiation and rests on the islanders' right to self-determination.
story.why: it revives one of the West's most sensitive territorial disputes at a moment when US backing for a close ally can no longer be assumed. (The Guardian, 04.09.2026; The Guardian — UK response, 04.09.2026)

story.headline: Nepal tunnel workers freed as water crisis grows
story.summary: Two workers were pulled alive from a Nepali hydropower tunnel nine days after a glacier-collapse flood; UNICEF warns 22,000 children lack safe water.
story.display_body: Rescuers pulled two workers alive from a Nepali hydropower tunnel on Friday 4 September, nine days after a Himalayan glacier-collapse flood, as UNICEF warned the disaster has left about 22,000 children without safe water. The flood was triggered by a glacier collapse on the Nepal–China border on 27 August (a glacial lake outburst flood — a wall of water released when a natural ice or moraine dam fails); the toll has since passed 1,270 across Nepal and China. UNICEF says damaged water systems and destroyed sanitation are raising the risk of waterborne disease in crowded shelters, and has sent water and hygiene supplies for around 19,000 people in the hardest-hit Rasuwa and Nuwakot districts.
story.why: the relief phase now turns on preventing a second wave of deaths from disease, in remote areas where roads, bridges and pipelines were swept away. (UN News / UNICEF, 03.09.2026 ; The Guardian, 04.09.2026)
